beats.trigger: From Personal to Team
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The hard part is not access; it is absorption.
beats.got: Giving people the tool is not the same as them using it, and the second part is the hard one.

beats.trigger: Walk in with one example where people had access to a tool or process but real use did not follow.
beats.got: I already have one: the dashboards the dispatch ops team was given and never opened.

beats.trigger: the likely adoption failure before it happens, including the social failure that's hardest to see
beats.got: nothing new, it's a list of verbs. The Christensen name-drop doesn't add anything.

beats.trigger: who's the one person who came to mind just now?
beats.got: My pricing analyst came to mind straight away, and I hesitate because she'd have to trust output I haven't checked myself.

beats.trigger: Your teammate doesn't want your agent. They want a job done.
beats.got: Start from what the teammate needs done, not from what I built.

beats.trigger: does it name one teammate, their current way of doing the job, and an outcome you could observe?
beats.got: A quick test for whether the job statement is real or generic. I'd apply it to my own briefs.

beats.trigger: Every picked candidate should name how it moves the teammate's outcome; infrastructure should appear only as a constraint.
beats.got: There are four things I can share, and 'share the context' is the one that fits my team's problem.

beats.trigger: You now have the teammate's job and a candidate selected against it.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: Now find the obstacle that decides whether the teammate can actually absorb it, then draft both halves of the plan.
beats.got: Next step is the obstacle, then a plan with a tech half and a people half.

beats.trigger: A good bottleneck explains why several other obstacles stay hard.
beats.got: Look for the one obstacle that makes the others hard, not the first limitation you notice. This is root-cause thinking and I'd use it.

beats.trigger: A polished technical file beside a people file full of unnamed roles is the finding, not a finished rollout.
beats.got: Unnamed owners are the result. It means I haven't actually got a rollout. That describes most of my team's AI work.

beats.trigger: checks the assumptions underneath these plans, imagines the failure
beats.got: nothing new, it's a signpost

beats.trigger: The technical and people plans are hypotheses.
beats.got: The plans are guesses to be tested.

beats.trigger: what would have to be true for this teammate, doing this job, to fire their current hire and use my candidate?
beats.got: Ask what would have to be true for them to switch. It's a Roger Martin question I know from consulting, and it's a better way to put it than 'how do I get adoption'.

beats.trigger: Six months from now, the teammate went back to the incumbent.
beats.got: A pre-mortem that ends in one named person, one question and one test for Monday. That is something concrete I can run.

beats.trigger: A candidate picked because it fits the infrastructure is shopping.
beats.got: Pick what moves the outcome, not what fits the platform. The point is fair but I've heard it already.

beats.trigger: The rest of this is about the person on the other end of your plan.
beats.got: nothing new

beats.trigger: The interview earned its keep when it found a third outcome past speed and quality
beats.got: Job first, candidate second again. The only new part is that a good interview finds something besides speed and quality.

beats.trigger: Hand someone the agent file and you have handed them the shell of a thing whose contents are still on your disk and in your head.
beats.got: What makes my setup work is the sources, the corrections and my judgement. The instructions file is the small part, so passing around prompts won't carry it.

beats.trigger: Accountability is the part with a name on it, and a name does not travel inside a folder.
beats.got: Context, boundary and checks can be copied. Someone still has to answer for it, and that person can't be copied.

beats.trigger: Access is a switch somebody flips, and it completes in a minute.
beats.got: nothing new. This is the big idea said a third time.

beats.trigger: Your agent runs on the part of your work you could never have written down.
beats.got: People take up things that look like something they already do. The Polanyi quote is decoration.

beats.trigger: The interface is the first piece whose shape depends on somebody whose calendar you do not control.
beats.got: The interface is the first part that depends on another person. It's a bit abstract.

beats.trigger: The leadership had not done the analysis. People they trusted had.
beats.got: A good analysis with a plausible proposal still died because the deciders hadn't done the thinking and the urgency moved. That is my CFO and my pricing pilot.

beats.trigger: Somebody they trust has to have used it first and said so.
beats.got: The conditions are small: it lands where they already look, it's right the first time, and someone they trust vouched for it. I can check all three.

beats.trigger: What you learned getting here is not one of the four things.
beats.got: nothing new. I don't follow the last sentence.

beats.trigger: If the agent reaches for a full rewrite anyway, push back
beats.got: The agent reviews and rewrites my sharing file, and I should make it edit only the section I name.

beats.trigger: Save the conversation. It's the bridge to when work resumes.

beats.trigger: Access is easy; absorption is scarce.
beats.got: nothing new, it's a recap

beats.got: Module 8 builds on whatever I test with one real person before it starts. They leave it up to me.

beats.trigger: What comes back from that contact is Module 8's raw material.
beats.got: nothing new

take_homes: Start from the teammate's job and write the outcome sentence before deciding what to share. Pick the form that moves that outcome, not the one that fits our platform.
Prompts and the agent file aren't what travel. The sources, the corrections and the judgement are, so the context needs a shared home that my fourteen people don't each copy privately.
A missing owner is the finding. Put one real name on each role, and test whether the person would switch from what they use now before building more.

monday.move: Put the pilot-cohort brief's sources, style notes and my list of corrections into one shared folder. Then ask the person who reads the brief first how she does that job today, and which of her current sources she'd drop if the brief were right the first time. Nothing gets built until she has answered.
monday.who: The analyst on the pricing working group who receives my pilot-cohort brief first. I'll settle which person it is Monday morning.
monday.when: Monday, 30 minutes before the pricing working group sync
monday.stop_condition: If she says her current spreadsheet or the CFO's weekly numbers already do the job and she wouldn't switch, I stop and rethink the job instead of building. If nobody will own the shared folder, I stop and escalate that first.
monday.blocker: We have no shared place for the context files. Everyone keeps their own copy, and I don't yet know which tool IT will allow for it given the customer data and GDPR questions.

misconception.why: The line about the agent file being only a shell made me see that the value sits in the curated sources, the corrections and my judgement, not in how well the prompt is written. I still think better prompting helps my own use, but it won't scale to my team.

one_line: Less about agents than about why nobody on your team picks up what you built. The story about the analysis nobody decided on was the best part, and the lecture says 'absorption not access' about four times too often.
